One Percenter Bikers: Highway 61 MC (Motorcycle Club)

content.p: Highway 61 is a New Zealand outlaw motorcycle club that began in Auckland in 1968 and grew into one of the country's largest. Its name comes from a Bob Dylan song, the NZ Herald reported, chosen in honour of a member killed in a road accident. By 2003 the same newspaper counted about 100 members in nine chapters, and called it the country's largest multicultural motorcycle gang. At least one chapter had by then opened in Australia.

The club's public record is mostly a record of courtrooms: a shooting in Christchurch, a stabbing in its own Auckland headquarters, a fatal ride on a state highway and a police drug inquiry in Wellington. The sections below follow those cases as courts and newspapers reported them. People are named as offenders only where a page shows a conviction.

The Herald's 2003 account says the club was formed in 1968 and registered as a motorcycle club in 1970. A hobbyist site on outlaw clubs, One Percenter Bikers, puts the founding in the same year and says its patch shows a skeleton gripping the handlebars of a motorcycle, with a road beneath. The same site calls the club one of the largest in New Zealand for decades.

The Australian dates differ by source. One Percenter Bikers says the club is believed to have reached Australia around 1984 and set up a Brisbane chapter in 1998. A criminologist writing in the Herald in 2019, Carl Bradley, wrote that Highway 61 set up chapters in Australia in the 1990s. A Herald report of June 2000 said Highway 61 had chapters "right through New Zealand and Australia". The sources do not agree on a single year, so none is given here.

Bradley's column placed the club in a wider traffic of bikers across the Tasman. He argued that Australia's policy of deporting convicted New Zealand citizens had helped Australian clubs such as the Rebels and the Comancheros establish themselves in New Zealand, and that the flow ran both ways, and named Highway 61's Australian chapters as an example of New Zealand clubs moving the other way.

A photograph in the Auckland War Memorial Museum's collection, taken by Robin Morrison and catalogued by DigitalNZ, shows members and associates of the Auckland chapter socialising around the bar at their headquarters. The museum's description calls the club an international outlaw motorcycle club with chapters throughout New Zealand.
content.h2: Police views of the gang scene
content.p: In June 2000 the Herald's Keith Perry reported that police believed formerly hostile motorcycle gangs were forming crime alliances. Police told him that gangs such as the Head Hunters and the Hells Angels picked the best of the smaller clubs as prospects. The article itself listed Highway 61 among groups with chapters across both countries. Auckland police gang intelligence officer Detective Cam Stokes said the big gangs were now choosy and wanted recruits who made money from illegal activities. The article said alliances were formed and broken regularly, and that rival gangs preferred to settle disputes peacefully because fighting interfered with making money. Those are the police's claims as reported, not findings of a court.

A New Zealand Police press release described Operation Fantail. A senior detective at the Organised Financial Crime Agency of New Zealand said it was the end of an 18-month investigation into the supply of methamphetamine and a drug known as fantasy in the lower North Island. Its second phase involved nine search warrants executed across Wellington City and the Hutt Valley. Police said they had recovered 200 grams of methamphetamine, 2,000 millilitres of GBH, $200,000 in cash and restrained assets worth $160,000, including sports cars and a Harley-Davidson. The detective said the operation showed that members of outlaw motorcycle gangs were financing large parts of the drug market in Wellington, the Wairarapa, Manawatü and Hawke's Bay, and that rival gangs were co-operating in the trade. Eight people arrested in the second phase were members or associates of Highway 61, police said, and were due to appear in the Wellington District Courts the following week. The page does not give the date of the operation or the outcome of those cases.
content.h2: The shooting of Max Shannon, Christchurch, 2000
content.p: On 8 August 2000 Max Shannon, a 25-year-old Black Power member, was shot as he sat in his car in Sylvester Street, Woolston, in Christchurch. Six people were originally charged with murder, according to the Christchurch Star report carried by the Herald in August 2001. One pleaded guilty in June that year. The other five were tried in the High Court at Christchurch over six weeks. One was discharged part way through and one was acquitted. Three, who had pleaded not guilty, were convicted and given life sentences.

Justice Chisholm set the minimum terms. He ordered 14 years for Matthew Bernard Grant, 37, who was described as the club's self-appointed leader in Christchurch. Dean Waka Nathan, 34, and Garth Geoffrey Bucknall, 32, who stood trial with Grant, each received 13 years. Murray Arnold Simms, 31, who had pleaded guilty, received 11. The judge called the shooting an "execution" that showed utter contempt for the law and for public safety, and called it another example of inter-gang conflict that had plagued the city.
content.h2: The killing of a national president, Manurewa, 2003
content.p: Kevin Paul Weavers, 43, a mechanic known as "Link", was national president of the club. He was found badly hurt at the Auckland headquarters in Holmes Street, Manurewa, early on the afternoon of Saturday 27 September 2003 and died in hospital about 1.20 p.m. The Herald reported that police feared the killing would lead to more violence, and that members from around the country were reported to be travelling to the headquarters. The headquarters stood in a light industrial zone, behind a metal fence and security cameras.

The Herald described Weavers' record: a 1984 charge, with two other men, over the rape of a woman in Howick; a clash, five years after that charge, between Highway 61 and Black Power that left five people in hospital with shotgun wounds; and a 1993 prison sentence of five years for receiving stolen cars worth $944,000 and for false pretences. The report did not say how the 1984 charge ended. It also recalled that member Bradley Haora had been shot dead at a gang property in Mt Eden in 1975, and that seven Hells Angels members were sentenced to up to ten years for it.

Police said at the time that Weavers' son Steven, 19, had been kidnapped for almost 24 hours in March 2003, beaten and stabbed, and later found by club members, and that they were looking at whether the two events were linked. They said they knew of no link.

Trial evidence, as the Herald summarised it in October 2004, painted a different chain of events. In September 2003 two friends of Weavers, Gary and Denise Turner, were invited to dinner at the Papakura home of Michael Brittain. A man arrived demanding money from the Turners, Turner was assaulted, and the couple blamed Brittain. Weavers then went to Brittain's home with three or four other men armed with hammers and beat him, breaking his arm and indenting his skull. Weavers also took Brittain's new Harley-Davidson, his car and his tools, the account said. In hospital Brittain said he would kill whoever put him there, the prosecutor told the court.

Brittain went to Kelly Robertson, a former president of the club's Otahuhu chapter. Weavers, as national president, had disbanded that chapter after the 1997 killing of Nomad gang member Malcolm Munns by a Highway 61 man; the prosecutor said it had drawn unwanted police attention, while Robertson said it was an amalgamation of two chapters. Robertson and a Highway 61 life member, Michael Gould, entered the headquarters about two hours after Brittain left hospital.

Robertson told the jury he went as a peacemaker to get the motorcycle back, and that Weavers, in a rage, attacked him with a double-bladed knife and stabbed himself in the thigh in the struggle. The Crown said that either he or Gould took the knife away; none was found at the scene. The jury rejected Robertson's account of self-defence. It convicted him of manslaughter and found Gould and Brittain not guilty of murder.

Sentencing Robertson, Justice Colin Nicholson said his offending was "very close to murder" and imposed 10 years with a minimum of six years and eight months, after taking a year off an 11-year starting point for medical reasons. He found that Robertson had taken a knife to the headquarters and took it away again so that police would not find it. The court heard that Robertson, 46, had 18 convictions going back to 1975 and had earlier been sentenced to three years for conspiring to supply methamphetamine.

Detective Senior Sergeant Mark Gutry, who led the homicide inquiry, told the Herald he believed the violence would have continued had Weavers survived. One Percenter Bikers lists the case in its timeline and says Robertson was seen on camera meeting Bandidos members around that time and was believed to be setting up a Bandidos chapter in New Zealand. The Herald pages opened for this account do not say that, and it is a claim of the hobbyist site alone.

One Percenter Bikers lists further episodes, which are given here as that site's claims. It says that in 1979 members of Highway 61 from Wellington clashed with the Lost Breed at a Nelson event, injuring four; that in 1983 two Head Hunters members were charged with the murder of Highway 61 member Steven Bliss before the charges were dropped when witnesses withdrew statements; and that in 2016 Brisbane police raided properties used by the club, including a clubhouse in Tingalpa, and charged seven people. It also names Malcolm Rewa, a former member, as convicted in 1998 of a series of rapes and given a 22-year minimum non-parole period. The site's own text counts those rapes as 25 in one place and 24 in another.

On 12 November 2017 a member, James Gregory Nelson, died when his motorcycle collided with a ute and trailer on State Highway 1 at Ohingaiti, north of Hunterville. Three members had been riding in what witnesses called "formation" after a club event in Tauranga that day. In February 2019 Judge Bruce Davidson, sitting alone, found James Eric Hiroki guilty of driving dangerously causing Nelson's death, along with further driving charges and a weapons charge. Leask was convicted of failing to stop to ascertain injury and render assistance, and was found not guilty of three charges of driving dangerously causing injury. Both were bailed to be sentenced on 22 March.
